name: Muchongoyo

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A local Ndau dance practitioner or cultural historian
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Stomp of the Ndau
This is Muchongoyo. Traditional.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (FtAsaEyPevY)
Title card: Muchongoyo · Zimbabwe · Traditional

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Originating with the Ndau people of Zimbabwe, the dance historically served as a preparation and celebration for warriors.
It has evolved into a presentational dance for community gatherings and cultural festivals.
on_screen: Map: Zimbabwe · Africa
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed at weddings, chief installations, harvest festivals, and burials of royals.
It is a secular dance used for entertainment and cultural celebration.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Danced in a cow horn formation, the performance involves synchronized foot-stomping, rhythmic clapping, and whistling.
It progresses from a solo introduction (Mungeneso) to group choreography (chibhubhubhu) and individual displays (chigiyo).
Watch for Mungeneso, chibhubhubhu, chigiyo.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (FtAsaEyPevY)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music relies on rhythmic drumming and vocal singing.
Women provide the vocal accompaniment and rhythmic clapping to support the male dancers.
Listen for the Drums.
The music is defined by the percussive sound of feet hitting the ground in synchronization, supported by drumbeats and vocal singing.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Verified recording — MISSING
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Rhythmic stomping and sharp claps
scenes.music: the music brief's underscore at its own tempo; drop narration under the hook of a verified recording if licensed, else original

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Men wear mbikiza, vests, feathers or ngututu, and leg/arm ornaments (zvihlabvu/machoba).
Women wear colored miniskirts (chikisa), beads (matimwa), and head coverings (maqeyo).
on_screen: Image gallery: 1 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Wilson Kumbula, Enock Porusingazi, Marcia Moyana, and Phillip Kusasa are credited with organizing galas and festivals that sustained the dance.
Known as Muchongolo among the Tsonga (Shangani) people.
A traditional Ndau dance, with variants found among the Tsonga people.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Muchongoyo is variant of Muchongolo: The Tsonga (Shangani) name for the same dance tradition.

music_brief.purpose: copyright-free soundtrack with the same DNA as the tradition's music — an original creation, not a reproduction
music_brief.sound_description: The music is defined by the percussive sound of feet hitting the ground in synchronization, supported by drumbeats and vocal singing.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Muchongoyo (Zimbabwe). Rhythm pattern: Rhythmic stomping and sharp claps. Instruments: Drums. Mood: energetic, rhythmic, celebratory. It should sound like this: The music is defined by the percussive sound of feet hitting the ground in synchronization, supported by drumbeats and vocal singing. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: the narrator wears the dance's traditional apparel, reconstructed meticulously and respectfully from the sources
